title: The Case of the Missing Apples
markdown:
“Well, this is peculiar,” Zara murmured, peering at a bare apple branch. The bark was cool under her fingers. The few leaves drooped. Last year these trees had dripped with apples — big rosy ones for pies and cider. This year: a few tiny things, no bigger than a ladybug’s egg. She tapped her chin, more serious than a misplaced sock. Apple season was the town’s highlight. A scarce harvest sat heavy.

Cora, perched on Zara’s shoulder, tilted her head, beady eyes scanning. “Chirp. Few apples. Very few.” Her voice was dry leaves on pavement. A glint near the roots caught her. “Shiny. No. Apple. Small.” She nudged Zara’s ear.

Teacher Lin knelt, gloves smelling of earth and sunshine. “The orchard is looking bare. The picnic relies on those apples. We need to figure out why. Fresh eyes, perhaps.” She smoothed her apron. The rows seemed to be holding their breath.

They walked the morning in a quiet procession, row after row, the picnic already imagined as empty plates. Zara, trail naturalist, held her small brass magnifying glass to twigs and leaves, hunting strange bugs or disease. Through the lens, leaf-hairs were miniature forests; dew sparkled and then rolled off, innocent. She checked a trunk for canker, a leaf for spots, a fallen petal for something that looked like trouble. Nothing useful. Cora flew ahead, darting through pink and white blossoms, then zipped back with chirps and head-bobs. Buds plump with promise. Healthy green leaves unfurling as if they had not heard about the picnic. No obvious villain. The trees had not forgotten how to make apples so much as they had forgotten to finish. The air, usually humming, felt strangely quiet, the sort of quiet that made Zara want a louder clue.

“Maybe we aren’t looking hard enough.” Disappointment sat in Zara’s stomach like a stone. Mysteries she could not solve made her tummy flip. A forest with no trails.

Cora had been busy from above. A flurry among the blossoms that ground-level had missed. “Buzz. Little buzzy things!” She flapped, a feathered announcement. “Flowers! Tiny legs! Yellow dust!” She landed and wiggled a foot: specks of gold on dark feathers.

Zara followed. A plump beetle, shell like a tiny emerald, crawled on a pink blossom. Golden powder clung to its legs, antennae, even its head. “Pollen.” Delighted whisper. “Teacher Lin — all over the beetle.”

The grains under the glass were stubborn yellow fairy-dust that refused to be a disease. Zara followed one beetle from blossom to blossom until it disappeared under a leaf. A breeze sighed through the orchard and more specks drifted, lazy golden leaves, flower to flower. “Moving. The buzzy things are carrying it. The wind too.” A message passed without anyone writing it down. She held the glass still until a second beetle arrived, equally dusty, equally uninterested in her theory.

Lin’s smile held a twinkle Zara knew meant the clue was real. “Insects visit for nectar. They pick up pollen like living backpacks. At the next flower, some rubs off. Another tree’s blossom, if we are lucky.” She pointed along the row, where a second variety waited with its own pink mouths open.

Cora bobbed. “Pollen. Flower to flower.”

“The wind helps when the insects rest. An apple blossom needs pollen from another apple blossom to start fruit. Without it, the flowers fall off.”

The thrill arrived, rare-bird-call bright. “Not enough buzzy things, or not enough wind — not enough pollen. That’s why so few apples.” Zara looked at beetles, little flies, a bee that had just landed, with a respect that had not been there at breakfast. Helpers. Apple-makers, if you wanted to be dramatic, which she almost did.

Lin did not call it a secret handshake or address budding scientists. She let Zara have the word. “Pollination.”

Cora puffed her chest. “We watched. We saw.”

Zara’s worry thinned. Looking closely, listening to Cora, walking the rows — that had been the work. She thought of the science club without making a speech: flowers that feed the visitors, care with sprays. Protect the apple-makers. Lin nodded once, which was enough.

They stood a minute longer in the quiet that was not quite as quiet now that they had names for the buzz. A bee worked a blossom as if the picnic depended on her, which, in a way, it did. Cora spotted a scrap of foil by the fence and zipped off, which was her own collection and not a lesson. Zara pocketed the magnifying glass and counted, roughly, the visitors she could see in one tree: not enough for last year’s dripping harvest, enough to start a plan. Next year’s picnic would still need weather and luck. It would also need beetles with dusty legs. She could work on that — flowers at the orchard edge, a word at science club, no sermon required.
